You might think asking an AI chatbot for medical advice is obviously a bad idea, but hundreds of millions of people do it every week.

In a now-lawsuit-worthy near-death case, ChatGPT advised a pastor to ignore symptoms of a pulmonary embolism—a condition with a 30% mortality rate. In fact, the chatbot's advice likely made things worse…

AI chatbots are useful for many things, but replacing a doctor's diagnosis is not one of them. Given their track record of confidently spouting nonsense, they're not even a good replacement for a Google search.

And yet, even OpenAI's own numbers show that hundreds of millions of people ask ChatGPT health questions every week. Similarly, an analysis of Microsoft Copilot search records found health queries were among the most common types of searches on the mobile app.

If you need any evidence of the potential consequences of relying on a chatbot for medical advice, a lawsuit filed by a Florida pastor offers a sobering example. The New York Times reports he is suing OpenAI after ChatGPT told him not to worry about symptoms of a pulmonary embolism.

ChatGPT told him to just get some rest. Not only did it discourage him from seeking medical attention—exactly the worst thing to do in this situation—but staying still for long periods is, in fact, the worst thing to do. I would know: I once developed a pulmonary embolism after a 12-hour flight following a broken bone; back then, researchers knew about the risk but hadn't yet told patients about it.

By the time Winters was finally taken to the ICU, doctors said his symptoms were likely the result of a series of pulmonary embolisms, worsened by weeks of sitting still on ChatGPT's advice.

Winters was reportedly using GPT-4o at the time, an older ChatGPT model known for its sycophantic responses. That may explain the trust-in-God language in the reply; but whatever AI model you use, don't let it give you medical advice.
